claim: The US Institute of Medicine establishes the Tolerable Upper Intake Level (UL) for vitamin D at 4,000 IU/day for all adults 19 years and older, including pregnant and lactating women
stance_target: Safety of 2000 IU/day Vitamin D3 (well below UL)
scope_conditions: US and Canadian populations, free-living healthy adults, chronic intake basis; IOM 2011
quoted_support: Adults 19 Through 30 Years of Age, Adults 31 Through 50 Years of Age, Adults 51 Through 70 Years of Age, Adults >70 Years of Age: UL 4,000 IU (100 μg)/day Vitamin D

claim: Vitamin D toxicity (hypercalcemia) is generally not observed below 10,000 IU/day in clinical studies; frank toxicity is frequently observed at 50,000 IU/day or more
stance_target: Safety of 2000 IU/day Vitamin D3 supplementation
scope_conditions: Multiple human clinical case reports and controlled studies compiled in IOM 2011 review
quoted_support: Doses below 10,000 IU/day are not usually associated with toxicity, whereas doses equal to or above 50,000 IU/day for several weeks or months are frequently associated with toxic side effects including documented hypercalcemia.
numbers: 10,000 IU/day NOAEL for vitamin D toxicity

claim: The IOM vitamin D UL of 4000 IU/day was derived by applying a 60% uncertainty reduction to the NOAEL of 10,000 IU/day, set 20% below 5000 IU/day identified in a single key study
stance_target: Scientific basis of 4000 IU/day UL for vitamin D
scope_conditions: IOM risk assessment framework for DRI UL derivation; 2011
quoted_support: Given the uncertainties surrounding the data and the reliance on a single report, the UL is set 20 percent below the level identified by Heaney et al. (i.e., 5,000 IU), specifically at 4,000 IU/day.

claim: The IOM recommends avoiding serum 25OHD levels above 125-150 nmol/L due to emerging associations with increased all-cause mortality, falls, and fractures
stance_target: Upper safe 25OHD blood level for vitamin D supplementation
scope_conditions: Based on observational studies and emerging data available to IOM committee 2011
quoted_support: Based on available reports, the committee considered that serum 25OHD levels above approximately 125 to 150 nmol/L should be avoided. Given the conclusion derived in Chapter 5 that bone health benefit is achieved by 97.5 percent of the population at 50 nmol/L, there is a range of serum 25OHD levels between 50 and 150 nmol/L that remains undescribed.
numbers: 50 nmol/L adequate for bone health in 97.5% of population

claim: Vitamin D toxicity symptoms include hypercalcemia, hypercalciuria, anorexia, weight loss, polyuria, heart arrhythmias, and eventually vascular/tissue calcification with renal and cardiovascular damage
stance_target: Vitamin D supplementation risks at excessive doses
scope_conditions: Clinical toxicology of vitamin D; hypervitaminosis D
quoted_support: Vitamin D intoxication generally presents with non-specific symptoms that may vary and often include anorexia, weight loss, polyuria, and heart arrhythmias. The condition eventually leads to vascular and tissue calcification with subsequent renal and cardiovascular damage.

claim: 2000 IU/day of vitamin D3 is well within the established safety margin, representing 50% of the tolerable upper intake level of 4000 IU/day
stance_target: Safety of Briyo Vitamin D3 2000 IU daily supplementation
scope_conditions: Derived from IOM 2011 UL standards; healthy adult general population
quoted_support: Intake values in the range of 4,000 IU/day would not appear to cause serum 25OHD levels to exceed 125 to 150 nmol/L, a concentration which is at the high end of the range of serum levels associated with nadir risk of outcomes such as all-cause mortality.
